title: Understanding the Azan (Call to Prayer)
summary: What the Azan actually is, a phrase-by-phrase breakdown of what it means, and why it's the natural starting point before learning Wudu and Salah.

body.text: The Azan is the call to prayer, recited aloud (traditionally by a muezzin, from a mosque) at the start of each of the five daily prayer windows. It serves two purposes at once: announcing that a prayer time has begun, and inviting anyone within earshot to come pray. It's the reason this lesson comes before Wudu and Salah in this app — the Azan is, in a real sense, the signal that starts the whole sequence you're about to learn.
The phrases, in order, with their meaning
The Azan is built from a small number of short, repeated Arabic phrases. Once you recognise them, you'll be able to follow along anywhere in the world, even before you speak any other Arabic.
This opens the Azan the same way it opens and threads through Salah itself — a declaration that nothing else competes with God's greatness, said before anything else.

body.arabic: أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
body.transliteration: Ash-hadu an la ilaha illallah (said 2 times)
body.translation: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah.
I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.

body.text: Together, these two lines are the Shahadah you met in Stage 1 — the Azan restates the core declaration of faith publicly, out loud, five times a day.

This pair is the actual invitation — literally calling people toward prayer, and describing that prayer as a path toward "falah," a word meaning success or flourishing in a deep, lasting sense, not just a worldly achievement.

For the Fajr (dawn) prayer specifically, one extra line is inserted here, said twice: "As-salatu khayrun minan nawm" — "Prayer is better than sleep." It's a gentle, practical reminder aimed at exactly the moment it's needed most.

body.translation: There is no god but Allah.

body.text: The Azan closes the way it began: with God's greatness and oneness, bookending the whole call.
What you're expected to do when you hear it

Simply hearing the Azan doesn't obligate you to drop everything that instant — the prayer window it announces typically lasts a few hours. Many Muslims pause briefly to quietly repeat the phrases along with the muezzin as a form of response, and it's traditional to recite a short dua afterward. Beyond that, it's simply your cue that it's time to plan for Wudu and Salah before the window closes — the very next two lessons.

body.question: Why does the Azan sound different in different countries or mosques?
body.answer: The words are the same everywhere (with only the Fajr addition and minor regional repetition-count differences between schools of thought), but the melody, pacing, and the reciter's individual voice vary a lot — there's no single "official" musical rendition, which is part of why the Azan can sound quite different from one mosque or country to another while saying exactly the same thing.

body.question: Do I need to physically go to a mosque every time I hear the Azan?
body.answer: No — praying at a mosque is especially encouraged and rewarded, particularly for men, but praying wherever you are (home, work, outdoors) is fully valid for each of the five daily prayers. The Azan is a reminder of the time, not a summons requiring your physical presence at a mosque every single time.

body.question: Have you already heard the Azan — recorded, at a mosque, or in a video — before starting this lesson? Now that you know what each phrase means, do you think you'll hear it differently next time?
